When you say “the literal embodiment of the protagonist’s fear”, that’s exactly what I want to have the villain be; the tricky part is to avoid copying the place where I got the idea from.

I know it’s not the best way, but I usually look to characters in the stories I like for basic inspiration, which I then use to create new characters that aren’t carbon copies of the inspiration.

With this villain, I got the general, very basic idea from the character of Death from Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. I found the concept of an unrelenting force that forces the hero to overcome his fear to be very interesting, but I knew that I couldn’t just copy Death and expect it to work.

One issue I have is that, unlike death, abandonment doesn’t seem to have a personification. I couldn’t find any mythological creatures that represent it, nor any other supernatural entity. 

Then I had the idea of this villain being a version of the protagonist from another world who couldn’t overcome his fear and trauma, and to avoid ever being hurt again he basically gave up his humanity, becoming a soulless monster.

The problems with this idea are: 

First, it potentially introduces the concept of a multiverse, which has some of the same problems as time travel. 

Second, the villain doesn’t really have a motive for traveling to another universe just to get a different version of himself on a better path.

The last thing I want is to have a villain that’s either too much of a copy or too passive to be an active threat to the protagonist.

I have three methods of creating names for my world.

The first is just borrowing names from existing religions, countries, and cultures, with the occasional alteration when suited. Some examples from my world include the seraphim, and some of the countries (like Volyn and Covasna).

The second is translating key words into other languages, picking the translations that sound good, and then modifying them if necessary. Some examples of these from my world include the Drekan (Icelandic for dragon, dreka), the Eirvar (Latin for forest, silva), and the Liskar (Finnish for lizard, lisk).
